The problem

Photo: Steffen Mokosch, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0, cropped. The store manager is an illustrative persona.

A store manager asks: which product categories generate the most revenue?

  • Her options today

    Wait about three days for an analyst, or weeks for a curated tool to be set up.

    Or learn the schema and SQL herself.

  • What she needs

    An answer today, the SQL behind it so she can check it, and her data never changed.

    Other tools pay for meaning in setup; this project pays in review.

  • Why it is hard

    Published scores fall from 91.2 % on Spider 1.0 to 21.3 % on enterprise tasks.

    “Revenue” is not a column: meaning is the hard part.

  • Who else it serves

    Managers new to a database, privacy-sensitive teams and teams with large schemas.

    Not for metrics that must match across teams.

How it works

One question’s path: one model call, two gates in code

Yellow is the model, teal is enforced in code. Only 79 of 608 stored values reach the model, never result rows; 45 of 45 read-only tests passed on 3 engines.

The 21 % trap: why she needs the SQL

“Which product categories generate the most revenue?”

The SQL, and what “completed revenue” adds
SELECT category, SUM(unit_price * quantity
+ * (1 - discount_pct)
FROM order_items JOIN products ...
+ JOIN orders ...
+ WHERE order_status = 'Completed'
GROUP BY category
All 220 orders, list price173,366
179 completed, discounted136,98421 % lower

Electronics revenue, same top category. Neither is wrong: the SQL shows the choice, and she decides.

What we measured

Local 9B model: 64.6 % on Spider, 35.2 % on BIRD

Spider dev64.6 % of 1,034
BIRD dev35.2 % of 1,534, with evidence
Demo suite4 of 12: too small to judge

Answers matching the reference rows; this project’s scorer, not leaderboard scoring.

On large databases, fewer tables scored higher

Every table + hints25.5 %, 8,501 tokens
Every table26.8 %, 6,221 tokens
Top 6 + neighbours29.1 %, 2,670 tokens

1,222 questions: +3.6 [+1.4, +5.8], about 2 s slower. A dropped table cut top 6 to 5.4 %; five later trials added no accuracy.

What is next

What the store manager should know before she trusts it

  • Measured limits

    About one answer in three did not match on Spider; nothing checks meaning.

    A missed table usually means a wrong answer; table selection is about 2 s slower.

  • Not yet tested

    Follow-up questions, other languages, and real company schemas of hundreds of tables.

    No user study yet, and running cost is not measured.

About one answer in three is still wrong: four tests come before any default changes

  • Business definitions

    Revenue stays ambiguous.

    Carry a definitions layer?

  • Targeted table recovery

    128 questions miss a table.

    Does recovery keep its gains?

  • New large schemas

    The gain is from 2 of 4 databases.

    Top 6 at every size?

  • A hosted model

    All results use one local model.

    Worth sending it the prompt?

A first, checkable answer for people who know the question but not the schema.
